instructions: Cut the 4 tbsp butter into small pieces and leave it on the counter to soften while you measure everything else.
In a large bowl, whisk the 2 cups flour, 2 tsp of the berbere, the 1 tbsp sugar and the 1 tsp salt.
Stir in 1/2 cup water a little at a time, until it comes together into a stiff, shaggy dough. Add a spoonful more water only if there's dry flour that won't pick up.
Add the soft butter and knead it in for about 5 minutes, until the dough is smooth and no longer greasy. Cover the bowl and let the dough rest for 10 minutes.
Cut the dough in half. Knead the last 1 tsp berbere into one half for anyone who likes it hotter, and keep the two halves apart from here on.
Roll each half into ropes about as thick as your little finger, then cut the ropes into 1/2 inch pieces.
Heat a large dry cast iron or heavy skillet over medium heat for 2 minutes. Add the mild pieces in one layer.

Cook them for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring every minute or two, until they're golden brown on all sides and rattle when you shake the pan. Transfer them to a plate and toast the spicy pieces the same way.
Let them cool completely. They get crunchier as they cool. Leftovers keep in an airtight container for up to a week.
Serve the mild and the spicy bites in separate bowls.
method_notes: All three make a stiff flour and water dough with a little sugar, salt and fat, cut it into small pieces and toast them in a dry skillet, stirring, until crisp on every side. Food.com (the lead) seasons the dough with berbere and kneads in soft butter; Fork and Salt adds ground warm spices, honey and niter kibbeh, and The Foreign Fork uses cayenne and oil. This follows the lead, but with 1 tbsp of berbere in place of its 2 tbsp, and only a third of that kneaded into half the dough so there's a mild bowl and a spicy one. No version had ratings to speak of (the lead shows 2 reviews and no rating count) and RecipeTin Eats has no dabo kolo, so the lead is the classic berbere and butter version among those read.
